### Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

Faced with the escalating complexity of cyber-cognitive threats, doctrinal reconstruction within national civil law must transcend the conventional boundaries of Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) regarding the validity of agreements. This is particularly crucial for the element of consent, which must be free from mistake or error (*dwaling*), duress, or fraud/deceit (*bedrog*). The doctrine of lawful cause (*causa yang halal*) and the absence of vitiated consent (*cacat kehendak*) must be interpreted in an evolutionary manner to encompass the doctrine of "cognitive sovereignty" (*cognitive sovereignty*). When a technology corporation deploys manipulative algorithms to hijack users' psychological autonomy in order to secure assent to terms of service, such consent is juridically flawed because it is obtained through covert undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) and the exploitation of structural vulnerabilities. Within the framework of civil law, this must be qualified as an unlawful act (*Perbuatan Melawan Hukum* / PMH) based on a doctrinal expansion of Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek). Here, damages are no longer defined solely in material or physical terms, but extend to the erosion of psychological integrity, cognitive fatigue, and violations of the right to think freely without deceptive algorithmic intervention.

The strengthening of this legal framework must also be aligned with cutting-edge international standards, such as the provisions set forth in the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689). Specifically, Article 5 thereof explicitly prohibits artificial intelligence practices that deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness to materially distort behavior in a manner that causes, or is likely to cause, physical or psychological harm. Furthermore, the interpretation of the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022)) must be broadened. The processing of personal data via psychographic profiling and predictive algorithms must be categorized as high-demand, high-risk data processing that rigorously safeguards data subjects' rights, including the right to object to decisions based solely on automated algorithmic processing (*automated decision-making*).

At the structural level, the establishment of an independent AI ethics oversight body—as mandated by multi-stakeholder governance models—must be endowed with robust quasi-judicial and administrative authorities. This body should comprise an interdisciplinary consortium of legal regulators, cyber-cognitive psychologists, technology ethics scholars, and civil society representatives tasked with conducting periodic algorithmic audits of AI systems operating within the Indonesian public sphere. Transparent reporting mechanisms for psychological manipulation violations must be instituted, enabling individuals and advocacy groups to file class-action lawsuits or administrative complaints against manipulative or addictive interface design practices. Consequently, corporations will no longer be able to hide behind the technical complexity of black-box algorithms to evade legal liability.

As a final synthesis of this discourse, the future of digital civilization hinges on our capacity to reclaim control over humanity's cognitive landscape. Law must not submit to technological determinism; rather, it must stand as a moral and normative bulwark affirming that technology is a secondary instrument for human flourishing, not the master of it. Through the harmonious integration of legislative reform (such as strengthening the interpretation of the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) and the doctrine of unlawful acts under Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)), the implementation of Value Sensitive Design, and collaborative, independent multi-stakeholder oversight, we can construct an artificial intelligence ecosystem that is not only innovative and globally competitive, but also fiercely upholds the dignity, freedom, and cognitive sovereignty of every citizen in the Republic of Indonesia.
